recipes.title: Choose a private desktop messenger that fits your contacts
recipes.description: Start with account setup, contact reachability and whether you need a mobile-linked account or an independent desktop identity.

picks.label: Existing Signal contacts
picks.reason: Desktop links into the Signal account and supports encrypted conversations, calls and files.
picks.tradeoff: Initial desktop use requires the mobile Signal account; it is not a federated chat client.

picks.label: Identity without a global user address
picks.reason: SimpleX is designed around contact connections rather than a global phone-number identity.
picks.tradeoff: Invitation and connection management differ from mainstream messengers; check the current desktop limitations.

picks.label: Peer-to-peer conversations
picks.reason: Jami provides distributed calling and messaging without requiring a conventional central chat server.
picks.tradeoff: Peer reachability, synchronization and account backup require a different workflow from cloud history.

picks.label: Session-network messaging
picks.reason: Session provides a distinct network and account-identifier approach for messaging.
picks.tradeoff: It does not interoperate with Signal or Matrix; assess the actual feature and network requirements.

recipes.title: Choose a Matrix client for your desktop
recipes.description: Use one Matrix account ecosystem while selecting a client whose platform maturity, media and calling coverage fit the task.

picks.label: Broad desktop and web access
picks.reason: Provides a full Matrix interface with official desktop packages and browser access.
picks.tradeoff: Homeserver and calling infrastructure are separate from client installation.

picks.label: Qt desktop workflow
picks.reason: Offers keyboard-oriented navigation, profiles and native desktop integration.
picks.tradeoff: Calling, codecs and secret storage differ by platform; the project qualifies encryption audit status.

picks.label: GNOME-focused Linux messaging
picks.reason: Combines Matrix accounts with an adaptive GNOME interface and rich message views.
picks.tradeoff: Official installation targets Linux and requires compatible secret-storage services.

picks.label: Conversation-focused interface
picks.reason: Emphasizes everyday messaging, spaces and rich media across established Linux/web deployments.
picks.tradeoff: Windows/macOS deployments were introduced as beta; calling requires compatible MatrixRTC infrastructure.

recipes.title: Choose an XMPP desktop or terminal client
recipes.description: Compare the client together with your server’s extensions: encryption, calls and file sharing are not identical everywhere.

picks.label: Graphical everyday XMPP
picks.reason: Brings modern messaging, files and account-provider choice into one desktop client.
picks.tradeoff: Check server extensions and macOS architecture availability.

picks.label: Focused Linux chat and calls
picks.reason: Keeps XMPP conversations and compatible calls in a streamlined GTK interface.
picks.tradeoff: Official distribution focuses on Linux and encryption must match the conversation configuration.

picks.label: Terminal and remote-shell use
picks.reason: Offers keyboard-driven rooms, encryption choices and plugins without a graphical desktop.
picks.tradeoff: Windows needs WSL or Cygwin and optional features depend on build configuration.

picks.label: Detailed configuration
picks.reason: Provides flexible windows, themes and optional encryption plugins for established XMPP users.
picks.tradeoff: Calling plugins and automatic updates differ across distributed builds.

recipes.title: Choose a softphone for an existing SIP account
recipes.description: A softphone is a client: check the SIP service, codecs and provisioning separately from the app’s price.

picks.label: Cross-platform SIP ecosystem
picks.reason: Offers a SIP-based communication client with open-source components and documented service integration.
picks.tradeoff: Service provisioning and account compatibility remain separate from installing the client.

picks.label: Compact Windows SIP calling
picks.reason: Focuses on Windows SIP calls with a small dedicated client.
picks.tradeoff: Windows-only scope and supported codecs may not match every provider.

picks.label: Commercial desktop workflow
picks.reason: Provides a SIP/IAX-oriented client with paid features and support paths.
picks.tradeoff: Free and paid editions have different capabilities and usage terms.

recipes.title: Choose voice chat for a community or game group
recipes.description: Decide whether the group wants a hosted community platform or a separately operated voice server.

picks.label: Self-hosted voice server
picks.reason: Pairs a desktop client with a server your group can operate and configure.
picks.tradeoff: Server hosting and voice setup remain your responsibility.

picks.label: Structured voice communities
picks.reason: Provides channels and permissions in a dedicated voice ecosystem.
picks.tradeoff: Client generations and server licensing limits need to match the planned deployment.

picks.label: Hosted text and voice community
picks.reason: Combines channels, media and voice in an established hosted service.
picks.tradeoff: Accounts, service policies and optional paid features are part of the choice.

recipes.title: Choose desktop access for a team chat deployment
recipes.description: These desktop apps connect to an existing workspace; evaluate the server and hosting plan as part of the decision.

picks.label: Topic-organized asynchronous work
picks.reason: Topics keep parallel discussions identifiable and the client supports several organizations.
picks.tradeoff: Teams must maintain the topic model and hosted history limits vary by plan.

picks.label: Managed Mattermost access
picks.reason: Supports several servers, notifications and administrator-provided settings.
picks.tradeoff: Desktop Apache licensing does not determine server production entitlements.

picks.label: Managed Rocket.Chat access
picks.reason: Connects users to organization-selected servers with desktop notifications and managed configuration.
picks.tradeoff: Server edition and version determine the actual collaboration features.

recipes.title: Choose browser or desktop video meetings
recipes.description: Compare participant access, hosting responsibility and organization requirements before choosing a meeting application.

picks.label: Browser-first open meeting stack
picks.reason: Provides browser-based meetings with public-service or self-hosted paths.
picks.tradeoff: Hosting, authentication and deployment configuration influence the actual meeting service.

picks.label: Hosted meetings across organizations
picks.reason: Offers desktop meetings and collaboration features with familiar guest workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Free meeting limits and paid entitlements vary by plan.

picks.label: Microsoft 365 collaboration
picks.reason: Fits organizations already using Microsoft identity, channels and collaboration services.
picks.tradeoff: Personal, work and education accounts have different capabilities and licensing.

picks.label: Managed business meeting workflow
picks.reason: Provides vendor-managed meetings and business collaboration options.
picks.tradeoff: Check the specific client package, account type and subscription feature set.

recipes.title: Choose an interactive virtual classroom
recipes.description: Lesson whiteboards, breakout activities and LMS integration can matter more than ordinary meeting features.

picks.label: Teaching and LMS integration
picks.reason: Combines shared presentations, whiteboards, polls and breakout rooms in a classroom-focused server.
picks.tradeoff: Supported hosting requires a dedicated Ubuntu server and ongoing administration or a hosting provider.

picks.label: Simpler open meetings
picks.reason: Works well for a browser meeting when classroom-specific analytics are unnecessary.
picks.tradeoff: Teaching workflows and LMS functionality require additional integration.

picks.label: Hosted classroom meetings
picks.reason: Provides a managed meeting service for classes that prefer vendor hosting.
picks.tradeoff: Education plans, recording and breakout entitlements must be checked separately.

recipes.title: Choose a general SDR receiver interface
recipes.description: Begin with the exact receiver hardware and OS, then compare multi-channel listening, plugins and recording needs.

picks.label: Modular multi-VFO listening
picks.reason: Provides multiple receive channels and hardware modules across desktop platforms.
picks.tradeoff: The project emphasizes nightly builds and device-driver compatibility remains essential.

picks.label: Focused analog-mode receiver
picks.reason: Offers AM/FM/SSB reception and spectrum inspection without designing a flowgraph.
picks.tradeoff: Supported hardware follows gr-osmosdr and package paths differ by OS.

picks.label: Windows station and recording
picks.reason: Combines multiple receivers, IQ playback and selected transceiver integrations.
picks.tradeoff: Commercial licensing differs from hobby use and transmit support is device-specific.

picks.label: Experimental multi-device workbench
picks.reason: Adds receiver/transmitter plugins and specialized demodulation in a configurable workspace.
picks.tradeoff: The project explicitly targets experimentation rather than mission-critical production.

recipes.title: Choose between legacy SDRuno and current SDRplay paths
recipes.description: Keep legacy configurations identifiable while checking hardware support before selecting a replacement.

picks.label: Current vendor cross-platform path
picks.reason: Offers graphical and headless operation on Windows, macOS and supported Linux systems.
picks.tradeoff: Original RSP1 is excluded and Linux support is narrower than all distributions.

picks.label: Existing legacy station
picks.reason: Retains the established SDRuno configuration and plugin workflow.
picks.tradeoff: The vendor marks it end of life; it is a legacy option rather than an active-development recommendation.

picks.label: Alternative receiver interface
picks.reason: Provides a modular receive interface where the appropriate SDRplay module and drivers support the device.
picks.tradeoff: Verify exact module/API and hardware compatibility; vendor parity is not assumed.

recipes.title: Inspect a captured radio protocol
recipes.description: Choose whether you need visual sample analysis, a structured protocol workbench or a programmable processing chain.

picks.label: Measure captured samples
picks.reason: Spectrograms and cursors help inspect modulation and symbol timing in recorded IQ files.
picks.tradeoff: It is an offline viewer, not a complete live capture and protocol decoder.

picks.label: Connect samples to message fields
picks.reason: Combines acquisition, demodulation, labeling and protocol interpretation for owned lab devices.
picks.tradeoff: Automatic decoding still needs a correct signal and protocol model.

picks.label: Build a custom decoder
picks.reason: Reusable processing blocks and flowgraphs let you express signal chains beyond fixed application features.
picks.tradeoff: Drivers and out-of-tree modules must match the selected GNU Radio generation.

recipes.title: Choose amateur-radio digital text workflows
recipes.description: Structured contacts, conversational text and broad modem collections solve different tasks.

picks.label: Structured weak-signal contacts
picks.reason: Implements timed modes such as FT8, FT4 and Q65 with documented operating sequences.
picks.tradeoff: Clock synchronization and short structured messages are central constraints.

picks.label: Alternative weak-signal workflow
picks.reason: Provides a separate WSJT-derived operating and decoding environment.
picks.tradeoff: Release cadence and supported features differ from WSJT-X; current maintenance is not assumed.

picks.label: Keyboard messages over HF
picks.reason: Uses JS8 message passing for free-form text through the current JS8Call-Improved continuation.
picks.tradeoff: JS8 messages are not ordinary FT8 contacts and need compatible peers.

picks.label: Several established text modems
picks.reason: Brings multiple sound-card digital text modes into one application.
picks.tradeoff: Choose a matching mode and configure the audio/rig path explicitly.

recipes.title: Choose digital voice or data software for a radio station
recipes.description: Identify whether the payload is speech, text or an experiment before comparing the interface.

picks.label: Open HF digital speech
picks.reason: Provides digital voice through an open codec/modem stack and a configured SSB station.
picks.tradeoff: Both ends need compatible modes and audio paths; development releases are not the stable channel.

picks.label: Text through audio modems
picks.reason: Supports multiple established text modes with station integration.
picks.tradeoff: It is not a speech-codec application and each mode has its own operating conventions.

picks.label: Custom signal experiments
picks.reason: Allows a purpose-built signal-processing chain using reusable blocks.
picks.tradeoff: Requires substantially more DSP and hardware integration work than a station-ready application.

recipes.title: Choose complementary software for an APRS station
recipes.description: Separate the sound-card modem from the mapping client; these roles can be combined in one station.

picks.label: Sound-card modem and gateway
picks.reason: Provides AX.25/APRS encoding, decoding and interfaces to client programs.
picks.tradeoff: A suitable audio/PTT setup is required and it does not supply a full map-focused interface.

picks.label: Extensible APRS maps
picks.reason: Displays station information using local maps and radio/Internet interfaces.
picks.tradeoff: Build paths and mapping dependencies require setup, especially on Windows.

picks.label: Java mapping and messages
picks.reason: Combines APRS mapping, local geographic data and extensible telemetry in a Java client.
picks.tradeoff: Java, map storage and external interface compatibility must be checked for the host.

recipes.title: Choose radio memory programming or live control
recipes.description: Channel memories and DMR codeplugs differ from live CAT control; match the tool to the exact model and task.

picks.label: Memories for supported radios
picks.reason: Offers one channel-editing workflow across a broad documented model list.
picks.tradeoff: Firmware variants, cable compatibility and per-model support remain decisive.

picks.label: Supported DMR codeplugs
picks.reason: Provides codeplug and contact-database editing on Linux and macOS.
picks.tradeoff: Only listed DMR models are supported and codeplugs are not universally portable.

picks.label: Live transceiver controls
picks.reason: Provides a dedicated CAT panel and fldigi integration.
picks.tradeoff: It controls operating settings rather than replacing every radio’s memory-programming application.

recipes.title: Choose an amateur-radio logbook
recipes.description: Compare general station records, integrated DX operations and contest-specific exchange handling.

picks.label: Linux-oriented SQL logbook
picks.reason: Combines contact records, QSL workflows and Hamlib/cluster integrations.
picks.tradeoff: MySQL/MariaDB setup is required and distribution packages can trail repository releases.

picks.label: Windows general station log
picks.reason: Provides contact, award and transceiver integrations for everyday operation.
picks.tradeoff: External service subscriptions and radio integration must be checked separately.

picks.label: Contest operation
picks.reason: Organizes contacts around contest rules, exchanges and station controls.
picks.tradeoff: A general daily logger can be simpler outside contests.

picks.label: Cooperating station applications
picks.reason: Combines modular logging, spotting, propagation and radio-control components.
picks.tradeoff: Several coordinated applications create more setup surfaces.

recipes.title: Choose satellite pass planning or signal decoding
recipes.description: An orbit planner predicts geometry; a receiver decoder processes the signal captured during a pass.

picks.label: Visual observation planning
picks.reason: Predicts passes, transits and selected flares with world and sky views.
picks.tradeoff: Use current orbital elements and correct site coordinates; it does not decode RF samples.

picks.label: Tracking and station coordination
picks.reason: Provides satellite tracking in a dedicated desktop application with supported station-control integrations.
picks.tradeoff: Radio/rotator setup and orbital data are separate requirements.

picks.label: Receive-data decoding
picks.reason: Turns supported live or recorded satellite signals into decoded products.
picks.tradeoff: Needs compatible RF hardware and supported signals; not every satellite has a decoder.

recipes.title: Choose a PLC programming environment
recipes.description: Compare editor openness, controller compatibility and runtime licensing as separate decisions.

picks.label: Open editor with simulator
picks.reason: Provides IEC programming and a simulator with multiple runtime targets.
picks.tradeoff: Bare-metal runtime and commercial deployment terms are separate from the GPL editor.

picks.label: Portable open PLC projects
picks.reason: Uses PLCopen XML with a compiler and several runtime options.
picks.tradeoff: Target I/O integration is engineering work and runtime licenses differ.

picks.label: Broad compatible-controller ecosystem
picks.reason: Offers IEC editors, libraries and device tooling for CODESYS-compatible targets.
picks.tradeoff: The free IDE includes a demo runtime; production runtime and add-ons can require licenses.

picks.label: Beckhoff PC automation
picks.reason: Integrates PLC engineering and supported industrial hardware configuration.
picks.tradeoff: Runtime/functions cost extra and VM operation does not provide hard-real-time guarantees.

recipes.title: Choose a robot simulator or offline programmer
recipes.description: General robot algorithms and production controller program generation require different interfaces and validation.

picks.label: Integrated robot learning and prototyping
picks.reason: Combines models, sensors, worlds and controllers in one environment.
picks.tradeoff: Model assumptions determine the usefulness of simulated behavior.

picks.label: Modular ROS-oriented simulation
picks.reason: Provides configurable physics, sensors and a plugin ecosystem for robot workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Linux support is strongest; ROS/version pairing and other-OS limitations matter.

picks.label: Scriptable robot scenes
picks.reason: Supports flexible scene scripting, external APIs and headless/library operation.
picks.tradeoff: Edu eligibility is narrowly defined; companies and general research institutions need other terms.

picks.label: Industrial offline programming
picks.reason: Adds controller post-processors and robot manufacturing workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Commercial program generation is licensed and actual workcells still need calibration and validation.

recipes.title: Choose a sender for a supported CNC controller
recipes.description: Check firmware and machine configuration before comparing convenience features such as probing, surfacing and browser control.

picks.label: Cross-platform desktop sender
picks.reason: Combines machine state, jogging and toolpath visualization.
picks.tradeoff: It is mainly a controller interface, so full CAM design remains separate.

picks.label: Guided Grbl/grblHAL workflow
picks.reason: Adds probing, surfacing and calibration helpers.
picks.tradeoff: Mach3/4 controllers do not use the supported interface.

picks.label: Autoleveling and G-code editing
picks.reason: Combines a sender/editor with probing-based surface compensation.
picks.tradeoff: Probe accuracy, units and controller settings directly affect generated motion.

picks.label: Browser interface near the machine
picks.reason: Keeps the serial server at the machine while exposing controls in a browser.
picks.tradeoff: The server and remote-access configuration must be maintained.

recipes.title: Choose software for electronic signal capture
recipes.description: Start with the acquisition hardware: these frontends have different device compatibility and protocol ecosystems.

picks.label: Open sigrok-compatible analysis
picks.reason: Provides logic/scope views and protocol decoders across supported sigrok devices.
picks.tradeoff: Device drivers and acquisition limits vary, and packages can be nightly builds.

picks.label: Saleae instrument integration
picks.reason: Offers an integrated capture/decoder workflow and automation APIs.
picks.tradeoff: Physical acquisition requires supported Saleae hardware.

picks.label: Analog Devices learning and analysis
picks.reason: Provides software instruments and control panels for supported ADI devices.
picks.tradeoff: Available tools depend on the exact device and plugin.

picks.label: Digilent multi-instrument suite
picks.reason: Combines analog/digital instruments and an SDK, with demo mode for exploration.
picks.tradeoff: Real measurements need compatible hardware and Linux installation includes the Adept runtime.

recipes.title: Choose a serial terminal or telemetry dashboard
recipes.description: Simple command exchange, terminal emulation and structured live visualization are separate needs.

picks.label: Simple data exchange
picks.reason: Provides text/hex serial send, receive and logging without full terminal emulation.
picks.tradeoff: Linux builds have limited developer testing.

picks.label: Linux command sessions
picks.reason: Separates command input and receive output and keeps device sessions.
picks.tradeoff: The current README only identifies Linux as tested.

picks.label: Windows terminal and scripts
picks.reason: Combines serial/SSH terminal emulation with a macro language.
picks.tradeoff: Windows-focused interface and macros do not transfer directly to other clients.

picks.label: Structured live dashboards
picks.reason: Turns parsed device frames into plots, gauges and recorded sessions.
picks.tradeoff: GPL source builds and official Pro binaries have different terms and industrial-driver availability.

recipes.title: Choose firmware update, chip programming or debug tools
recipes.description: A supported vendor update, an external flash programmer and a debug server are different operations.

picks.label: Supported device firmware updates
picks.reason: Uses the Linux firmware-update ecosystem for devices supported by its plugins and firmware sources.
picks.tradeoff: Availability depends on the exact device and vendor-provided update support.

picks.label: Supported flash-chip access
picks.reason: Reads, writes and verifies chips through documented internal or external programmers.
picks.tradeoff: Unsupported hardware, especially laptops, is explicitly warned against; Windows internal programmers are unsupported.

picks.label: ST device programming
picks.reason: Provides GUI/CLI programming and device configuration for supported STM32 targets.
picks.tradeoff: Target-specific settings can be persistent and require exact device documentation.

picks.label: Debug-probe integration
picks.reason: Connects supported JTAG/SWD probes and targets to GDB and programming workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Probe/target scripts and host drivers determine compatibility.

recipes.title: Choose Linux process tracing or a persistent audit trail
recipes.description: Select the observation model: an attached process, a wider captured event stream or a policy-driven persistent audit log.

picks.label: Trace one process or failure
picks.reason: Reveals syscalls, signals, missing paths and error returns without rebuilding the app.
picks.tradeoff: Tracing affects timing and output may include application data.

picks.label: Capture container-aware system events
picks.reason: Adds reusable traces and context for Linux container troubleshooting.
picks.tradeoff: Needs a compatible probe/driver and careful capture scope.

picks.label: Keep configured attributable events
picks.reason: Collects kernel audit records and offers structured query/report tools.
picks.tradeoff: Only configured events are collected, and backlog or storage pressure can lose data.

recipes.title: Choose configuration assessment or file-integrity monitoring
recipes.description: A configuration scan, an integrity baseline and event collection provide different evidence.

picks.label: Specified SCAP baseline
picks.reason: Evaluates machine-readable security policies and generates structured results.
picks.tradeoff: Applicable current content is required and upstream Windows support has been removed.

picks.label: Broad local assessment
picks.reason: Reviews many system configuration areas and records improvement findings.
picks.tradeoff: Recommendations still require interpretation for the system’s actual purpose.

picks.label: File-integrity baseline
picks.reason: Compares selected filesystem metadata/content against a previously captured database.
picks.tradeoff: A trustworthy baseline and update procedure are necessary; it does not explain every change by itself.

picks.label: Recorded action history
picks.reason: Collects rule-selected events that can help attribute later changes.
picks.tradeoff: Rules, storage and lost-event monitoring must be configured deliberately.

recipes.title: Choose an OpenVPN desktop client
recipes.description: All choices need a server or service. Compare OS support, simultaneous tunnels and configuration control.

picks.label: Vendor-managed profile access
picks.reason: Imports profiles from compatible servers and provides a documented desktop client.
picks.tradeoff: Only one active server connection at a time; Linux uses a separate client.

picks.label: Open-source macOS interface
picks.reason: Provides a no-charge GPL macOS frontend with bundled supporting binaries.
picks.tradeoff: Profile options must match the selected stable release and macOS networking behavior.

picks.label: Advanced native connection control
picks.reason: Adds simultaneous tunnels, split DNS, routing and scriptable deployment.
picks.tradeoff: It is a paid client and advanced routing still requires network knowledge.

recipes.title: Choose Wi-Fi inspection, site surveying or passive monitoring
recipes.description: Match the measurement method to the question; network names alone do not establish physical coverage.

picks.label: Nearby-channel and capability inspection
picks.reason: Shows channel overlaps, network details and signal history using a Mac adapter.
picks.tradeoff: Standard and Pro editions differ; it is not a full heatmap survey tool.

picks.label: Coverage surveys and planning
picks.reason: Builds licensed survey/heatmap/planning workflows from site measurements.
picks.tradeoff: Edition limits, commercial rights and measurement quality matter.

picks.label: Passive wireless monitoring
picks.reason: Collects observations from supported Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/RF sources into a web interface.
picks.tradeoff: Adapters and drivers dominate compatibility; Windows is a WSL/remote-capture workflow.

recipes.title: Choose cross-brand RGB control
recipes.description: Check your devices first, then compare effect design, licensing and release maturity.

picks.label: Open cross-brand device control
picks.reason: Provides a common interface for supported RGB devices.
picks.tradeoff: Hardware support and access permissions must be verified for the exact device.

picks.label: Integrated lighting and paid content
picks.reason: Combines effects, reactive content and device controls with a free core.
picks.tradeoff: Linux is beta, standard use is personal/noncommercial, and Pro/content purchases have separate entitlements.

picks.label: Conditional layered effects
picks.reason: Offers plugins and data-driven profile layers for custom reactive lighting.
picks.tradeoff: PolyForm Noncommercial is source-available, and prerelease device support has uneven testing.

recipes.title: Choose GPU controls for your operating system
recipes.description: Select by supported GPU/driver and control scope; no software guarantees a safe or faster tuning result.

picks.label: Linux GPU control comparison
picks.reason: Provides a current Linux-oriented alternative for supported GPU control workflows.
picks.tradeoff: Check exact GPU/driver features instead of assuming every control is available.

picks.label: Existing Linux profile workflow
picks.reason: Applies hardware profiles per application on supported devices.
picks.tradeoff: Upstream is maintenance-only and does not plan new hardware support.

picks.label: Windows card monitoring and tuning
picks.reason: Combines monitoring, supported tuning controls and fan profiles.
picks.tradeoff: Capabilities vary by board/driver and stability must be assessed on the actual hardware.

recipes.title: Choose USB sharing for a remote host
recipes.description: Choose by operating systems, device timing and licensing, then verify the actual peripheral workload.

picks.label: Windows USB host with supported clients
picks.reason: Shares Windows-attached USB devices through its documented USB/IP workflow.
picks.tradeoff: Client support and device/driver behavior must match the intended setup.

picks.label: Cross-platform licensed server
picks.reason: Provides desktop client/server packages and a free client.
picks.tradeoff: The paid server license is bound to hardware and cannot be transferred.

picks.label: Alternative cross-platform product
picks.reason: Provides remote USB sharing across its listed desktop platforms.
picks.tradeoff: Current free-homepage and purchase-page pricing conflict; Linux kernel compatibility is also unresolved.
